summary:
The Central African Republic poses serious risk to a trans or gender-nonconforming visitor. No provision of national law recognises gender identity or protects a person from discrimination on that basis, and the United States State Department's 2023 Human Rights Report records no legal anti-discrimination provisions covering LGBTQI+ persons at all.

Legal gender recognition is not permitted in the Central African Republic. A visitor whose passport or other travel documents carry a marker inconsistent with their presentation has no domestic route to align them, and no official process exists through which a changed marker would be issued or honoured.

The penal code does not explicitly criminalise consensual same-sex relations between adults. Article 85 instead criminalises attacks on public morals, and conduct of that kind in public draws harsher penalties than the other offences covered by the same public-morals provisions. For a visitor the operative effect is exposure: any visible same-sex or gender-nonconforming conduct in public leaves them liable to arrest on morals grounds, and the harsher penalty band attaches specifically to the public setting.

The constitution defines marriage as a union between one man and one woman, and same-sex marriage is banned. A visitor travelling with a partner therefore has no recognition of that relationship in any official proceeding, and public affection between same-sex partners falls back on the public-morals provisions.

There is no support infrastructure to fall back on. The 2023 human rights report states that LGBTQI+ persons cannot serve openly in the military, that the criminalisation of same-sex activity in public has pushed the community underground, and that no organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights are known to exist in the country. A trans visitor who is harassed, assaulted or detained has no domestic body to appeal to.
tangentialFactors:
Sexual-orientation and gender-identity questions remain taboo in the Central African Republic and are widely characterised as imported from Europe and contrary to African values. That framing shapes how a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor is likely to be received by the public as well as by officials.

Protection machinery exists at the international level without any corresponding domestic implementation. The country received two recommendations in a previous Universal Periodic Review cycle concerning non-discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity and the situation of sexual minorities, and stakeholder submissions to the review held in January 2024 again carried SOGI-related recommendations.

Detention carries risks that extend well beyond the morals provisions. A United States State Department report documented extrajudicial killings, torture and rape by security forces and by Seleka rebels, together with harsh prison conditions. That report contained little LGBT-specific material, so the conditions it describes are not measured against the treatment of gender-nonconforming detainees specifically.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the same absence of protection that shapes visitor risk, but on a permanent basis. There is no legal route to recognition of a person's gender, no anti-discrimination provision covering employment, housing, health care or public services, and no possibility of serving openly in the military.

With no organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights known to operate in the country and the community driven underground by the public-morals provisions, residents have no established channels for reporting abuse, securing legal assistance or organising collectively. Confidential support has to be sought outside national structures.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory records that ILGA World's 2023 survey 'Our Identities Under Arrest' covers the Central African Republic, but does not carry the survey's Central African Republic-specific findings. What that survey establishes beyond the penal-code position described here is unresolved on the present sourcing.

No prosecution data is available. Whether Article 85 is applied against individuals in practice, at what frequency, and whether gender-nonconformity alone is treated as an attack on public morals are all unresolved, and the sources describe a community pushed underground rather than documenting cases.

The 2012 human rights report predates the 2023 material by a decade and carries almost no LGBT-specific content. Its findings on state violence and prison conditions cannot be read as a current measurement, and the relationship between those findings and the treatment of detained gender-nonconforming persons is not established.

The scope of the military exclusion, including whether it bears on a foreign visitor's status in any way, is not specified in the sources.
